unit.title: Taxes on your investments
unit.description: How much you pay Hacienda (Spain's tax authority) when you invest in Spain, and how to pay only what's fair, legally

u31l1.title: The savings base and its bands

texts: Band by band, not all at once
You sell at a profit. The gain goes into the **savings base** of IRPF (Spanish income tax), which is taxed **in bands**: each slice at its own rate.
You make €8,000 selling shares. How is it taxed?
The first €6,000 at 19 % and the rest at 21 %
Nothing up to €50,000
Find the gain at which the last euro starts paying 23 %.
Moving up a band **only makes the part above the limit more expensive**. With a €50,500 gain, the last euro pays 23 %, but your average rate is 20.8 %.
That 23 % only applies to whatever is above €50,000.
The first €6,000 still pay 19 %.
Raise the gain and watch the bands
Ana's fund
Ana
My fund has made €15,000 this year! I haven't sold anything.
I'm going to pay a fortune on my tax return, aren't I?
How much does Ana pay on that gain?
About €3,000, on the savings scale
She'd only pay if she sold. Without selling, there's no gain to declare.
Nothing until she sells or redeems
Exactly! That deferred tax keeps investing for her: **tax deferral**.
19 % of the fund's whole value
Even when you sell, you don't pay on everything: only on the gain.
What about dividends and interest?
Those are taxed in the year you receive them, with 19 % withheld upfront.
Savings or general?
IRPF has two bases. Where does each kind of income go?
Savings base
General base
Dividends from shares
Income from your savings: savings base.
Interest from a deposit
Also income from capital: savings base.
Gain from selling an ETF
A gain from a sale: savings base.
Your salary
Income from work: general base.
Cashing in a pension plan
When you cash it in, it's taxed as income from work.
Gain from selling bitcoin
Crypto sold at a gain: savings base.
Sort the six kinds of income.
Interest, dividends and gains from selling shares, funds, ETFs or crypto go into the **savings base**. Your salary and cashing in a pension plan go into the **general** one.
Does it come from your work or from your savings?
Sort each kind of income

steps.title: The savings scale (2026)
steps.body:
• Up to €6,000: **19 %**
• €6,000 to €50,000: **21 %**
• €50,000 to €200,000: **23 %**
• €200,000 to €300,000: **27 %**
• Over €300,000: **30 %**

This is the common-territory scale. The Basque Country and Navarre have their own rules; always check with the Agencia Tributaria (Spain's tax agency).
steps.key: Investments are taxed in the savings base, from 19 % to 30 %, and gains only when you sell.
steps.tip: Hacienda gets paid when you sell at a profit, not when your portfolio goes up.

texts: Losses count too
This year you make **€5,000** selling some shares and lose **€3,000** on others.
How much are you taxed on?
On €5,000: losses don't count
Losses on sales **are subtracted** from gains on sales in the same year: €5,000 − €3,000 = €2,000.
Now you make €8,000. How big a loss do you need for all of it to be taxed at 19 %?
A declared loss **lowers your taxes**: with an €8,000 gain, a €2,000 loss leaves the base at €6,000, all at 19 %. That's why it's worth declaring sales at a loss too.
Base at zero: this year you pay nothing on your sales.
Part of your gain already pays 21 %.
Move the gain and the loss
Is it a sale for Hacienda?
Only what you **sell or swap** is taxed. Does this create a gain or a loss this year?
Yes: it's a sale
Not taxed yet
You sell shares at a profit
Gain = sale value − purchase value, fees included.
You swap bitcoin for ether without going through euros
It's an exchange: it counts as a sale.
You sell an ETF at a loss
A realised loss: you can use it to offset gains.
You buy more shares
Buying isn't taxed.
Your fund rises 20 % and you don't sell
Unrealised gain: not taxed until you sell.
You move euros from your bank to your broker
Moving your own money isn't earning anything.
Sort the six moves.
**Gain = sale − purchase**, including the fees on both. If you bought in several goes, **FIFO** applies: the ones you bought first are sold first.
Has something left your portfolio in exchange for something else?
Sort each move
The leftover loss
Pablo
This year I made €4,000 on some shares and lost €6,000 on others.
I also got €4,000 in dividends. Is the leftover €2,000 of loss just wasted?
What do you tell him?
Yes, it's wasted
No: the law lets him use it in two ways.
Part comes off the dividends and the rest off the following years
Exactly: up to **25 %** of the dividends; the rest, over **4 years**.
Hacienda gives him €2,000 back in cash
There's no refund: the loss only reduces what he's taxed on.
After those 4 years, any loss you haven't used expires.
The December trick
Leo
I've got a trick: on 30 December I sell at a loss so I pay less.
And on 2 January I buy the same thing back. Sorted.
Does it work?
Yes: the sale was in December
He's buying the same thing back within two months: the law stops that.
No: the loss is deferred until he sells what he bought back
Exactly. He doesn't lose it, but he'll have to wait.
No: it's illegal and he'll be fined
Selling isn't illegal. He just can't use the loss yet.
It's the **two-month rule**: article 33.5 of the IRPF Act.
Look two months **before and after** the sale. If it isn't listed, one year.
Does the rule apply?
A loss has to wait if you buy **homogeneous securities** (the same ones) in the two months before or after the sale.
Loss deferred
Doesn't apply
You sell an ETF at a loss and buy the same one back 3 weeks later
Within the two months after.
You sell at a loss and buy the same thing back 3 months later
Outside the window: the loss counts now.
You bought more of the same share a month before selling at a loss
The window looks backwards too.
You sell at a profit and buy back the next day
It only affects losses: you're taxed as normal.
You sell a share at a loss and buy one from a different company
They aren't homogeneous securities.
You sell unlisted shares at a loss and buy back 6 months later
For unlisted securities, the period is one year.
Decide all six cases.
The rule **doesn't punish: it defers**. It only affects losses, and the loss is applied when you sell the securities you bought back.
Two questions: is it a loss? Are you buying the same thing back inside the window?
Decide each case

steps.title: Legal optimisation
steps.body:
Before the year ends, some investors realise losses to offset gains, respecting the two months (for example, switching to a different product that tracks a similar index).

It's legal, but tax should never be the main reason for an investment.
steps.key: If you buy the same thing back within two months, the loss has to wait.

texts: From the pricey fund to the cheap one
Marta
I've got €20,000 in a bank fund that charges 1.8 %. I'm €6,000 up.
I want to switch to an index fund at 0.2 %. How do I do it?
What do you tell her?
Redeem and buy the index fund with the money
She'd pay €6,000 × 19 % = **€1,140** for no reason.
Request a transfer from the index fund's provider
That's it! She switches funds without paying anything now.
Stay in the expensive one to avoid tax
No need: the transfer exists for exactly this.
In a **transfer** (a Spanish «traspaso»), the money goes from fund to fund without passing through your account.
You keep the original purchase date and price. You only pay when you actually redeem.
Without paying tax?
Transfers work between **investment funds**. Can you do this without paying tax now?
Yes, by transfer
No, it's taxed
Rebalancing between two index funds
Fund to fund: transfer.
Selling an ETF to buy another
Even though they're funds inside, ETFs are taxed on every sale.
Switching fund manager
You request it at the new manager and it isn't taxed.
Selling shares to buy a fund
Selling shares is always taxed.
Moving from an equity fund to a money market fund
Both are funds: transfer.
Redeeming to your account and buying another fund
If the money passes through your account, it's no longer a transfer.
Sort the six moves.

**Funds:** tax-free transfers. **ETFs:** taxed on every sale, like a share (except for one very limited technical exception). If you hold for years without touching anything, the difference is small; if you move your portfolio around, it matters.
Is it fund to fund, without passing through your account?
Sort each move
The value of deferring
If you transfer instead of redeeming, the **€950** of tax you don't pay today stays invested (7 % a year, an example, not a promise).
What does that €950 grow into over 20 years?
About €1,900
About €3,700
About €19,000
At 7 %, money roughly doubles every 10 years: twice in 20. That's **€3,676**.
Take it to 20 years.
Deferring tax **compounds** too. You'll pay in the end, but on a bigger snowball: a transfer is like changing lanes without paying a toll.
Almost four times as much! Without lifting a finger.
Drag the years
The W-8BEN form
Your broker
You're going to receive dividends from US companies. Do you want to sign the W-8BEN form?
What do you do?
Sign it
Good: the US will withhold **15 %**, the treaty maximum.
Skip it, more paperwork
Without it, the US withholds **30 %**, and here you can only deduct 15 %.
I'll sign it next year
Meanwhile, every dividend loses 30 % at source.
And then I pay again in Spain?
It's taxed in Spain (19-30 %), but you deduct what you paid there: that's relief for **international double taxation**.
At most the treaty %, and never more than you'd pay here.
This year or when you sell?
What you **receive** is taxed when you receive it. What **rises without being sold** isn't. When is each one taxed?
Taxed this year
Not until you sell
Dividend received from a share
You receive it: taxed this year.
An accumulating ETF that reinvests dividends
It reinvests inside: you're not taxed until you sell.
Interest from a deposit
You receive the interest: it's taxed this year.
A fund that rises 20 % without you selling
Unrealised gain: nothing until you sell.
Dividend from a distributing ETF
It pays it out to you: taxed when you receive it.
Sort all five.
**European accumulating ETFs and funds** reinvest dividends inside and you aren't taxed until you sell. And a dividend isn't free money: the price drops by roughly that amount.
Does the money land in your account or stay inside?
Sort each case

steps.title: When they withhold too much
steps.body:
Some countries withhold more than the treaty allows: Switzerland, **35 %**. Getting the excess back means paperwork over there.

European accumulating ETFs and funds handle this internally.
steps.key: Sign the W-8BEN if you receive US dividends, and deduct double taxation in your tax return.

texts: Which form applies?
If you hold **more than €50,000** abroad, Hacienda wants to know. Which form applies on 31 December?
Modelo 720
Modelo 721
Neither
€70,000 in shares with a foreign broker
Securities abroad worth more than €50,000: Modelo 720.
€80,000 in crypto on a foreign exchange
Crypto held abroad worth more than €50,000: Modelo 721.
€200,000 with a Spanish broker
It's in Spain: these forms are for what you hold abroad.
€30,000 in an account at a foreign bank
It doesn't reach €50,000.
A €90,000 flat in France
The 720 also covers property abroad.
€20,000 in crypto on a foreign exchange
It doesn't reach €50,000.
Sort the six cases.
The **720** covers accounts, securities and property abroad; the **721**, crypto held abroad. They're **information returns**: filing them doesn't cost you any tax.
First: is it outside Spain? Then: is it over €50,000?
Sort each case
Ten swaps, zero euros
Bruno
This year I've made ten swaps between cryptos. I've never cashed out into euros.
So I've got nothing to declare, right?
What do you tell him?
Of course: no euros, no gain
Every swap between cryptos is a sale for Hacienda.
Every swap is a sale: work out the gain or loss on each one
Exactly. Keep a record of the date and the euro value of every trade.
Declare only the one that made the most
You have to declare them all. And losses help you offset, too.
Buying and holding isn't taxed. Selling or swapping is: from 19 % to 30 %.
And remember: crypto **can be lost entirely**. It isn't protected like a deposit.

steps.title: Reporting isn't paying
steps.body:
• **Modelo 720** (Spanish foreign assets return): from January to March. After that, only if the value rises by more than €20,000 or you no longer hold those assets.
• **Modelo 721:** crypto held abroad worth more than €50,000 on 31 December.

In 2022 the Court of Justice of the EU struck down the disproportionate penalties of the 720, but **the obligation to report remains**.
steps.key: Investments abroad above €50,000 must be declared, even if they don't generate any tax.
steps.tip: A foreign broker can be cheap, but the paperwork with Hacienda is on you.

u31l1-1.prompt: You sell shares at a gain of €8,000. How much do you pay under the savings scale?

u31l1-3.prompt: A gain of €20,000 from selling a fund. How much do you pay?

u31l1-4.prompt: You sell at a gain of €10,000. How much do you pay?

u31l1-5.prompt: Match each band of the savings base with its rate.
u31l1-5.explanation: Combined national and regional scale in force in 2026 in the common territory.

u31l1-8.prompt: With a gain of €10,000 you pay €1,980. What's your average rate? (one decimal place)
u31l1-8.explanation: 1,980 ÷ 10,000 = 0.198 → 19.8 %. The average rate is always below the rate of the top band.

u31l1-10.prompt: Which regions have their own IRPF rules?
options: The Canary Islands and the Balearic Islands
u31l1-10.explanation: They have a special (foral) regime. Everywhere else (the common territory) the national scale plus the regional one applies.

u31l2-1.prompt: You buy 100 shares at €20 with a €10 fee and sell them at €30 with another €10 fee. What's your taxable gain?

u31l2-2.prompt: You buy 10 shares at €50 and, months later, another 10 at €80. You sell 10 at €90. Using FIFO, how much do you gain? (no fees)
u31l2-2.explanation: FIFO: you sell the first ones, the €50 ones. 10 × (90 − 50) = €400.

u31l2-4.prompt: In the previous case, how much do you pay on that €2,000 net gain?
u31l2-4.explanation: 2,000 × 19 % = €380. Without offsetting, you'd have paid on €5,000: €950.

u31l2-7.prompt: Put in order how a loss on a sale is used.
options: Whatever remains, over the next 4 years
It's subtracted from gains on sales in the same year
What's left over, from dividends and interest up to 25 %
u31l2-7.explanation: After four years, any unused loss expires.

u31l2-9.prompt: If you bought in several goes, the first ones you bought are treated as sold first: the ____ method.
u31l2-9.explanation: First in, first out: what comes in first is what goes out first.

u31l3-1.prompt: What does the two-month rule do?
options: It forces you to hold shares for two months
It bans selling at a loss in December
It defers the loss if you buy the same securities two months before or after selling them
u31l3-1.explanation: It stops people selling just to pay less and then buying straight back.

u31l3-4.prompt: Bruno bought more shares in a company on 15 February. On 1 March he sells the ones he already had at a loss. What happens?
options: He loses the shares bought in February
Nothing, the rule only looks at what you buy afterwards
The loss is deferred because he bought identical securities in the previous two months
u31l3-4.explanation: The rule looks at the two months before and the two months after the sale.
feedback: He doesn't lose anything: the tax use of the loss is just delayed.
What you bought in the two months before the sale counts too.
That's it: the window runs two months backwards and forwards.

u31l3-7.prompt: The rule applies if you buy ____ securities, that is, the same ones you sold.
u31l3-7.explanation: For example, shares in the same company or the same ETF.

u31l3-8.prompt: You sell at a loss on 15 October. How many months do you have to wait to buy the same thing back without the loss being deferred? (listed securities)
u31l3-8.explanation: The window is two months: if you buy back after 15 December, it no longer kicks in (as long as you didn't buy the same thing in the two months before the sale).

u31l3-9.prompt: What's true about the two-month rule? Select all that apply.
options: It bans selling within two months of buying
It defers the loss, it doesn't cancel it
It's in Article 33.5 of the IRPF Act
u31l3-9.explanation: You can sell whenever you like; what changes is when you can use the loss.

u31l4-1.prompt: Match each product with how it's taxed.
u31l4-1.explanation: Each vehicle has its own tax rule.
right: Tax relief when you pay in, taxed as employment income when you cash out
Can be transferred tax-free until you redeem

u31l4-2.prompt: Your fund went from €10,000 to €15,000. If you redeem it to buy another one, instead of transferring, how much tax do you pay?
u31l4-2.explanation: Gain: €5,000. 5,000 × 19 % = €950. With a transfer, you'd pay €0 now.

u31l4-3.prompt: How much tax do you pay when you transfer from one fund to another?
u31l4-3.explanation: The tax is deferred until you finally redeem.

u31l4-6.prompt: Put in order how a transfer between funds works.
options: You place the transfer order with the destination provider
The money moves from fund to fund without touching your account
That provider requests the money from the original one
u31l4-6.explanation: You start it at the destination; you don't have to sell anything at the origin.

u31l4-9.prompt: Paying the tax later so that money keeps investing is called tax ____.
u31l4-9.explanation: It's legal and it's the big advantage of transfers.

u31l5-1.prompt: You receive a gross dividend of €1,000 from a US company and you've signed the W-8BEN. How many euros does the US withhold?
u31l5-1.explanation: 1,000 × 15 % = €150, the maximum under the Spain–US tax treaty.

u31l5-2.prompt: Following the case: in Spain you owe 19 % (€190) and you deduct the €150 paid in the US. How much more do you pay in Spain?
u31l5-2.explanation: 190 − 150 = €40. In total you pay €190: you don't pay twice.

u31l5-3.prompt: If you don't sign the W-8BEN, how much does the US usually withhold from your dividends?
u31l5-3.explanation: And in Spain you can only deduct up to the treaty's 15 %: you lose the rest unless you claim it back over there.

u31l5-7.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u31l5-7.explanation: With these four concepts you understand almost all the tax on foreign dividends.
right: Deduction so you don't pay twice
Reinvests dividends without you being taxed until you sell
Form for the reduced US withholding rate

u31l5-9.prompt: Pablo receives dividends from a Swiss company. Switzerland withholds 35 % and the treaty with Spain only allows 15 %. What happens to the difference?
options: To get the excess back he has to claim it from Switzerland, with all the paperwork
He deducts all of it in Spain
u31l5-9.explanation: Some countries withhold more than the treaty allows. That's why many people prefer accumulating funds.
feedback: Exactly: the extra 20 % has to be claimed from the Swiss tax authority.
In Spain he can only deduct up to the treaty's 15 %.
It isn't automatic: you have to apply for it.

u31l6-1.prompt: You swap 0.5 ether for solana without going through euros. What is it for Hacienda?
options: A sale that can produce a gain or a loss
Nothing: it only counts when you go back to euros
u31l6-1.explanation: Every swap between cryptos is taxed on the difference between its cost and its value at that moment.

u31l6-2.prompt: In which cases would you have to file Modelo 720? Select all that apply.
options: €40,000 in an account at a foreign bank
€55,000 in crypto on a foreign exchange
€60,000 in shares with a broker based in Germany
u31l6-2.explanation: The account doesn't reach €50,000. Crypto abroad goes on Modelo 721, not 720.

u31l6-3.prompt: Modelo 721 is for crypto held in custody abroad worth more than €50,000 on 31 December.
u31l6-3.explanation: It's existed since 2024 and, like the 720, it's for information only.

u31l6-4.prompt: You buy 0.1 bitcoin at €30,000 per bitcoin and sell it at €60,000 per bitcoin. How much tax do you pay? (no fees)

options: In June, with your income tax return
u31l6-7.explanation: From 1 January to 31 March, based on your situation on 31 December of the previous year.

u31l6-10.prompt: The information return for crypto held in custody abroad worth more than €50,000 is Modelo ____.
u31l6-10.explanation: The 720 is for accounts, securities and property; the 100 is the income tax return; the 303 is for VAT.
